Hunt
HUNT
v.t.
From Anglo-Saxon huntian, to chase or pursue game. Webster 1828: to chase wild animals for the purpose of catching or killing them; to pursue with hostility. Scripture’s gravest use of the word has souls, not beasts, for the quarry.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel’s indictment of the false prophetesses is the most chilling use of the word in Scripture, because of what they were hunting: Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes, and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls! Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive that come unto you? (Ezekiel 13:18). They were not persecuting anyone. They were supplying comfort — pillows and kerchiefs, soft things — and the LORD calls the trade soul-hunting. Proverbs describes the same predation in another form: by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life (Proverbs 6:26). The ordinary use is Esau’s: Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it (Genesis 27:5), the errand that gave Jacob his opening. And David complains of a king’s disproportion: the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains (1 Samuel 26:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HUNT as to chase wild animals, particularly quadrupeds, for the purpose of catching or killing them; to pursue with hostility; to follow closely; to search for diligently.

expand to see more

HUNT, v.t. — To chase wild animals, particularly quadrupeds, for the purpose of catching them for food, or for the diversion of sportsmen.

To pursue; to follow closely; as, to hunt a man from place to place.

To use, direct or manage hounds in the chase.

HUNT, v.i. — To follow the chase; and figuratively, to search diligently, with for or after.

Anglo-Saxon huntian, to hunt; related to hentan, to seize.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 13:18 — "And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes, and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls! Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive that come unto you?"

Proverbs 6:26 — "For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life."

Genesis 27:5 — "And Rebekah heard when Isaac spake to Esau his son. And Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it."

1 Samuel 26:20 — "Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains."

Modern Corruption

Ezekiel 13 identifies soul-hunting not with persecution but with the supply of comfort, and it is the passage most needed against a preaching that has made reassurance its whole business.

expand to see more

The women of Ezekiel 13 sew pillows and make kerchiefs. Their offence is not cruelty; it is softness — upholstering the consciences of people God was calling to repent. The chapter has already named the men who did the same thing with words: they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace (Ezekiel 13:10), daubing a flimsy wall with untempered morter. That is the exact shape of the modern therapeutic pulpit, which has learned to speak fluently of a hearer’s pain and hardly at all of his guilt, and which measures a sermon by whether people left feeling better. God’s verdict on the trade is that it hunts souls. The kindest thing that can be said of a man under God’s displeasure is that he is under it, and the preacher who withholds that has not spared him anything.

The second half of Ezekiel 13:18 is the searching question: Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive that come unto you? The two activities are set against each other. A ministry that hunts cannot also save alive, and there is no neutral middle where a man merely fails to help. This is why the Reformed tradition has insisted that the law be preached before the gospel — not because it enjoys severity but because a pillow under the arm of a man on the edge of the pit is the cruellest object in the world. Proverbs 6:26 shows the same predation in the seduction of the adulteress, who hunts for the precious life: the word Scripture uses for the soul’s value is the same word it uses for what the hunter is after.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsud (H6679), to hunt or lie in wait for; tsayid (H6718), game or venison; radaph (H7291), to pursue.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsud (H6679) — to hunt, to lie in wait; to hunt souls (Ezekiel 13:18) and the adulteress hunting the precious life (Proverbs 6:26).

Hebrew tsayid (H6718) — game taken in hunting, venison; Esau’s errand (Genesis 27:5).

Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — the soul or living being; the quarry of Ezekiel 13:18.

Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue or chase; the parallel verb for hostile pursuit.

Hebrew tapel (H8602) — untempered, insipid; the worthless morter of the same chapter (Ezekiel 13:10).

Usage

"Sew pillows to all armholes... to hunt souls! (Ezekiel 13:18) — the offence is softness, not cruelty."

"Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive? (Ezekiel 13:18) — the two are set against each other, with no neutral middle."

"The adulteress will hunt for the precious life (Proverbs 6:26) — the word for the soul’s worth is the word for the quarry."
